extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and practitioners interested in evaluating scientific and anthropological claims (readers of Popular Science Monthly; historians of science; anthropologists; general scientifically literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging the validity of empirical claims and theoretical interpretations in natural philosophy and anthropology — e.g., assessing travelers' accounts of social customs or judging Goethe's color theory against Newtonian optics. Emphasizes evidential strength, correct interpretation of observations, experimental procedure, and scholarly conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength and competency of evidence and witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence, therefore, ought to be of the very strongest, and the witnesses fully competent to deal with the facts they narrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand strong, well-attested evidence for wide-reaching inferences (e.g., when treating polyandry as an extensive system). Prefer witnesses who have had full opportunities to observe the underlying customs rather than casual travelers. Example: Mr. McLennan's broad inferences require the very strongest evidence and competent witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution with travelers' accounts and potential misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming our opinions as to the customs of savage tribes, ... the accounts given by travelers must be received with caution. They may state quite correctly each fact they observe, but they are very likely to be wrong in their interpretation of its meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat raw factual observations from travelers as potentially reliable in detail but suspect in interpretation; verify underlying social structure before drawing conclusions. Example: Schurmann's observation of two men living with one woman was recorded as polyandry but was group-marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct classification of social forms (distinguish group-marriage vs true polyandry)
rubrics_metrics.description: When our information is incomplete, it must often be far from easy to distinguish between communal marriage and true polyandry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require detailed ethnographic information about clan, exogamy/endogamy, and marital rules to classify a marriage system. Avoid treating cohabitation or multiple sexual partners as proof of polyandry without structural evidence (e.g., clan rules, recognized husbandhood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate prevalence vs exceptional cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Not a few of Mr. McLennan's instances of so-called polyandry admit of a similar explanation ... in every case the men were of a clan which intermarried with that of the woman, the circumstances were exceptional, and the custom was not the general practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish occasional or convenience practices from systemic social institutions; require evidence that a custom is tribe-wide or normative before treating it as the system of marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal logical and demographic plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere arithmetical difficulty in the way appears to me to be insurmountable ... under such a system it is evident that ... so many times more numerous must the men be than the women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check theoretical proposals for demographic and logical coherence (e.g., whether a proposed widespread system would imply unrealistic sex ratios or social consequences). Use simple quantitative reasoning to test plausibility of claims (example: polyandry-as-system implies far more men than women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative explanations and avoid unwarranted survival narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of the Levirate ... does not appear to me to have anything at all to do with polyandry ... there is no need for us to look upon it as a survival of anything at all, and ... it would serve very well as a survival of group-marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting historical or customary phenomena, evaluate multiple hypotheses rather than assuming one historical derivation (e.g., do not assume Levirate derives from polyandry when group-marriage could explain it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require full acquaintance with underlying causes before trusting testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: No witness here is to be trusted unless he has had very full opportunities of making himself acquainted with that which underlies the custom he describes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor observers who engaged sufficiently with the social context to know rules, meanings, and motivations behind observed behaviors; devalue superficial or short-term observations for deep cultural claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly courtesy and temper in scientific debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a writer permits himself to use words such as these, he should be very sure that he has firm ground under his feet; and even then it would be better to leave them unsaid. There is nothing in any line of scientific research to make a man of undoubted learning and ability forget the courtesy which he owes to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain respectful tone and avoid contemptuous scorn when critiquing other scholars; ensure criticisms are founded on solid evidence before strong language is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of demonstration over opinion in science
rubrics_metrics.description: In the region of science, where demonstration instead of opinion is paramount, such differences ought hardly to be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize demonstrable, reproducible results and logical deduction rather than personal or rhetorical argument. Scientific claims should be backed by demonstrative evidence; disagreements require experimental or logical resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory must follow from facts, not facts be forced to fit theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe began at the wrong end, inverting the true order of thought, and trying to make the outcome of theory its foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid circular reasoning where theoretical preference dictates interpretation of observations. Use empirical data to form and test theory; do not select or reinterpret facts merely to support a prior theoretical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of careful, varied observation but beware of overreach in explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as Goethe remained in the region of fact his observations are of permanent value. But by the coercion of a powerful imagination he forced his turbid media into regions to which they did not belong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect broad, careful observations (they can be valuable), but constrain speculative extrapolation and ensure interpretations stay within what the data legitimately support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for precise scientific definition and rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: The headings alone indicate the enormous industry of the poet; showing at the same time an absence of that scientific definition which he stigmatized as 'pedantry' in the case of Newton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clear, exact definitions and rigorous conceptual distinctions in scientific writing over vague, poetic, or symbolic headings that impede precision and falsifiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish objective from subjective experiments and control for perceptual effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The experiment being then 'objective.' It is sometimes looked at directly through the prism, the experiment being then 'subjective.' ... He possessed a full and exact knowledge of the phenomena of subjective colors, and described various modes of producing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that separate objective physical measurements from subjective perceptual phenomena; account for physiological effects (retinal persistence, subjective colors) when interpreting observational results (e.g., prism viewing, colored fringes at boundaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of experimental setup and boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: In the production of chromatic effects, he dwells upon the absolute necessity of boundaries — 'Grenzen.' The sky may be looked at and shifted by a prism without the production of color; ... the colors being confined to the edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to experimental configuration (backgrounds, edges, boundaries) because setup can produce or suppress effects; report and control these conditions when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate relevant physical theory when interpreting observations
rubrics_metrics.description: He by no means understood the physical action of turbid media, but he made a great variety of experiments bearing upon this point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established physical theories (e.g., optics, scattering in turbid media) to interpret experimental observations rather than rely solely on descriptive analogy; seek interdisciplinary knowledge to explain phenomena (example: understanding why turbid media appear blue by reflection and yellow by transmission).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heed expert critique and established demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Both these effects are immediately deducible from Newton's theory of colors. But this, though explained to him by physicists of great experience and reputation, Goethe could never be brought to see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to correction by domain experts and to well-established demonstrations; when experienced practitioners show a demonstration deduces an effect from accepted theory, re-evaluate one's contrary interpretation rather than dismiss expert explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish descriptive observation from theoretical conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater part of the first volume is taken up with Goethe's own experiments, which are described in nine hundred and twenty paragraphs duly numbered. It is not a consecutive argument, but rather a series of jets of fact and logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate the cataloguing of observations (useful descriptive data) from the construction of coherent theoretical argument; avoid presenting scattered facts as if they constitute a persuasive theoretical demonstration without synthesis.
